tier_reason: Third-party Gazebo-classic benchmark (scpeters/benchmark boxes test, CSV test_results/BENCHMARK_boxes_model_count.csv and pdf/roscon2014_scpeters.pdf) with public code but no CPU model, compiler, flags or engine versions, from a 16-star repo that is not a well-known suite; same evidence and tier as the catalog's ODE and Simbody entries.

corrections.claimed_speedup: test_results/BENCHMARK_boxes_model_count.csv timeRatio (wall time / simulated time, lower is faster), Bullet vs DART vs Simbody vs ODE: 101 boxes, collision flag 1: 1.4384 vs 7.22947 vs 1.87016 vs 1.3357; 101 boxes, flag 0: 1.47622 vs 4.37142 vs 1.84033 vs 1.58186; 81 boxes, flag 0: 1.1899 vs 3.1365 vs 1.48602 vs 1.23362; 1 box, flag 0: 0.127279 vs 0.136993 vs 0.12391 vs 0.101879. Derived from page data: Bullet about 5.0x faster than DART at 101 boxes with flag 1 and 3.0x with flag 0, and faster than DART in all 12 configurations (1.08x to 5.0x); Bullet 1.25x to 1.30x faster than Simbody at 81 and 101 boxes and faster in 10 of 12 configurations, but Simbody is about 3% faster at 1 box (0.12391 vs 0.127279 and 0.125744 vs 0.129334) while taking half as many steps (dt 0.001 vs 0.0005); Bullet faster than ODE only at 101 boxes flag 0 (about 1.07x) and 81 boxes flag 0 (about 1.04x), slower than ODE in the other 10 of 12 (for example 101 boxes, flag 1: 1.3357 vs 1.4384, ODE about 1.08x faster; 1 box, flag 0: ODE about 1.25x faster). ROSCon 2014 slides, Benchmark 3 object stacking, 'Time ratio (real / sim)': ODE 0.4, Bullet 0.5, DART 1.1, Simbody >100.
corrections.caveats: Numbers are from a third-party Gazebo-classic benchmark by OSRF engineers (repo scpeters/benchmark, Apache-2.0, 16 stars; README asks for Gazebo 6 or later and states no compiler, flags, CPU, or Bullet/DART versions) and the ROSCon 2014 slides (pdf/roscon2014_scpeters.pdf), roughly 2014-2015 vintage; Bullet runs through Gazebo-classic's Bullet plugin, so Gazebo overhead is included and the measured Bullet is whatever version Gazebo linked then, not the current bullet3 tree. The wins are over DART and Simbody, not over ODE (Gazebo's default engine): ODE is faster than Bullet in 10 of 12 box configurations and in the stacking test (0.4 vs 0.5); Bullet wins only at 81 and 101 boxes with collision flag 0, by about 4% and 7%. Simbody beats Bullet at 1 box (about 3%) even with a 0.001 s step against 0.0005 s, so the Simbody rows are not step-matched; DART's angular momentum error in the same CSV is 2.36521 against 0.00626 for Bullet, so the DART rows are not accuracy-matched either. Same benchmark source as the catalog's ODE and Simbody entries. The bullet3 README and docs carry no benchmark numbers of their own. A search summary (snippet only) of Erez, Tassa and Todorov, ICRA 2015 (Bullet, Havok, MuJoCo, ODE, PhysX) says no gaming engine led clearly on speed; the paper itself was blocked. Last commits 2026-10-09 are README-only; the last non-README change is 2025-10-22 (add pyproject.toml), the last code PR merges 2024-04-09.

notes: Real third-party numbers that match the CSV, but the claim overstated two details: Bullet is not faster than Simbody in all 12 configurations (Simbody wins at 1 box, both collision flags) and the 81-box win over ODE is about 1.04x, not 1.07x; tier stays C. Shortcomings: slower than ODE (Gazebo's default) in 10 of 12 box rows and in stacking; no CPU, compiler, flags or engine versions; Gazebo overhead included; DART and Simbody rows not accuracy- or step-matched. Not a duplicate; shares its benchmark with the ODE and Simbody entries.

tier_reason: First-party Google Benchmark output on the project wiki (benchmark code public in Benchmark/BenchmarkMain.cpp, Box2D rows behind the commented-out BENCHMARK_BOX2D define), but no compiler, flags, build type or exact CPU model, so C.

corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from the project's GitHub wiki page; neither the README (which says only that the project is 'benchmark assessed', linking to Wikipedia) nor Benchmark/README.md links to it. Compiler, flags and build type are not stated for the run (Benchmark/README.md recommends -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and warns 'Don't put much weight into these results unless you're clear on the code that's being timed'); the hardware is only '2.6 GHz Intel Core i7', 8 X 2600 MHz CPUs. The Box2D rows exist only if BENCHMARK_BOX2D is defined by editing Benchmark/BenchmarkMain.cpp (the define is commented out at line 85) and Box2D is linked by hand with an unstated build; Box2D 2.4.1 is named for the earlier 00991d1ec run, not for the ef285b19a run. The scenes are small microbenchmarks: WorldStepWithStatsStatic steps a world of shapeless static bodies only, and in DropDisks the disks are spaced 2 m apart with radius 0.5 so no contacts form (measures integration and broad phase, not contact solving). PlayRho's default StepConf uses 8 velocity and 3 position iterations, matching Box2D's Step(1/60, 8, 3). The same page's earlier run (commit 00991d1ec) showed PlayRho about 100x faster on AddPairStressTest400/18 (1,120,420 ns vs 104,630,145 ns), which the author called surprising and not trustworthy; the later run gives 2.2x. Wins are mixed: PlayRho loses both TilesRestComboGround rows (/12 by about 1.2x, /36 by about 1.07x). The only comparison is against Box2D v2, its own ancestor (PlayRho began as a port of Box2D 2.3.2); no comparison with Box2D v3 exists. Last commit 2024-04-30, so stale.

notes: All claimed rows match the wiki's ef285b19a run exactly; tier C holds (first-party, no compiler, flags, build type or CPU model). Shortcomings: degenerate microbenchmark scenes (static-only world, contact-free disks), Box2D build and version unstated for the cited run, mixed results (loses TilesRestComboGround), only compared with the older Box2D v2 line, stale since 2024-04-30. Fixed caveat: the README does not point to the wiki benchmark page.

tier_reason: Numbers known only from a search summary of Boost trac ticket #6135 (trac.cpp.al, svn.boost.org, lists.boost.org and listarchives.boost.org all failed with ENOTFOUND); a user's bug-report timing with no compiler, flags or CPU is at best C, and snippet-only evidence stays at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Boost trac ticket #6135 (Boost.Random patch proposal by Jan Drugowitsch, November 2011; snippet only): generating 100 million gamma variates, GSL about 22.3 million samples/s against Boost.Random gamma_distribution about 5.4 million (Boost using Knuth's method, GSL Marsaglia and Tsang 2000), about 4.1x (derived from page data); with the ticket's patch Boost reached about 14.5 million samples/s against GSL about 22.7 million in the same run, about 1.6x (derived from page data), the remaining gap attributed to GSL's Ziggurat normals versus Box-Muller.
corrections.caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: the figures come from a WebSearch summary of Boost trac ticket #6135; trac.cpp.al, svn.boost.org and both Boost mailing-list archives fail with getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND here, so the ticket text, compiler, flags, hardware and Boost version were not seen (the ticket is from November 2011). The patch was apparently never merged: Boost.Random's current gamma_distribution.hpp (develop branch) still says 'The algorithm is taken from Knuth' and uses tan()-based rejection for alpha > 1, so the 2011 gap may still apply to current Boost, but no current measurement was found. GSL's randist/gamma.c uses Marsaglia-Tsang with gsl_ran_gaussian_ziggurat. libstdc++'s std::gamma_distribution already uses Marsaglia-Tsang (bits/random.tcc) with polar-method normals, so GSL's edge over the C++ standard library is unmeasured and would come only from Ziggurat versus polar normals. Other snippets do not show GSL winning: a 2012 Rcpp Gallery post timed GSL's Mersenne Twister Gaussian draws slower than R's rnorm and Armadillo; S. Gerlach's PRNG slides reportedly rate GSL fastest for Gaussian sampling but no numbers were visible. No evidence was found for GSL beating a BLAS/LAPACK or FFT incumbent (the lead's guessed category fft is wrong). GSL is GPL-3.0-or-later (copyleft; linking GSL makes the combined work GPL). repo_url is the gnu.org project page (www.gnu.org ENOTFOUND here); the GitHub copy github.com/ampl/gsl (GPL-3.0, 639 stars, 288 commits, CMake build and AMPL bindings) carries the GSL 2.8 NEWS and was last committed 2026-05-19, which reflects AMPL's packaging, not upstream GSL.

notes: Snippet confirms the ticket numbers (GSL 22.3 vs Boost 5.4 Msamples/s; after patch GSL 22.7 vs Boost 14.5), so C stays, but nothing was opened first-hand and there is no compiler, flags, CPU or Boost version. The record's caveat that Boost's gamma sampler was 'since fixed' is wrong: Boost develop still uses Knuth's method, while libstdc++'s std::gamma_distribution already uses Marsaglia-Tsang, so GSL's win is over Boost only. Shortcomings: snippet-only 2011 evidence, single distribution, GPL copyleft, upstream last_commit unknown.
